claims.claim: The blogger says the novel's first epigraph reads exactly like the opening of a real-world country's textbook.
claims.quote: reads exactly like how a textbook of a real world country

claims.claim: The blogger judges that same epigraph, taken by itself, informative but boring.
claims.quote: A pretty informative, yet boring, introduction epigraph
claims.page: immediately after the quoted first epigraph

claims.claim: The blogger marks the move from epigraph to main text as a tonal shift, asking why the narrator writes about himself instead of the facts.
claims.quote: But what is this tonal shift?
claims.page: commentary after the two quoted opening paragraphs

claims.claim: A reader who has finished all sixteen books names the chapter-opening excerpts describing aspects of Six Duchies history or culture as one of the things she loved.
claims.quote: the excerpts at the start of each chapter describing some aspect
claims.page: section on Assassin's Apprentice / the Farseer trilogy

claims.claim: The same reader names the categories of concrete detail she noticed on a second reading: clothing, customs, politics and architecture.
claims.quote: details that she includes on clothing, customs, politics, and architecture

claims.claim: The same reader reports that details which read as thrown-in description always return later with relevance, and that she read watching for them.
claims.quote: simply throwing in random details of description, always come back
claims.page: section on the Fitz and the Fool trilogy

claims.claim: The same reader names what she finds appealing in the Bingtown Traders: that everything among them is a negotiation and a conversation.
claims.quote: everything is a negotiation and a conversation
claims.page: section on the Liveship Traders trilogy

claims.claim: The reviewer says Hobb does not define the magic word for word but shows it slowly, as if it were the most natural thing.
claims.source: Omnilegent: A Need to Read, 21 June 2020
claims.quote: doesn’t come out and define it word for word for you

claims.claim: Hobb's own rule for a passage she finds boring is to compress it rather than write it, and she says a chapter may be one sentence long if the writer wants.
claims.quote: You can have a one sentence chapter if you want
claims.page: section "I don't want to write the next scene. It's boring."

claims.claim: Hobb supplies her own model sentence for compressing four days of travel, which states the duration, its cost and the arrival at a small holding near a water hole.
claims.quote: After four days of punishing travel, they reached a small
claims.page: section "I don't want to write the next scene. It's boring."

claims.claim: Hobb advises a paper thesaurus over a word processor's synonym tool, on the ground that the software offers the same synonyms every other writer is using.
claims.quote: the same synonyms that every other writer is using

claims.claim: Hobb's own example of the editing pass that unblocks her replaces a general adjective with a specific one, correcting a red car to candy apple red with metal flake.
claims.quote: The car isn't red, it's candy apple red with metal flake

claims.claim: The reviewer names what Hobb spends pages on that most epic fantasy does not, including worrying about the apprentice fees for dependants and whether an old friend is going senile.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel blog, review of The Golden Fool
claims.quote: worrying about the apprentice fees for dependants
claims.page: review of 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', Originality section

claims.claim: The same reviewer states the book's governing rule as personal: motivations are personal and consequences will also be personal, the fantasy mattering because of the reality in its shadow.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel blog, review of The Golden Fool
claims.quote: motivations are personal, and that consequences will also be personal
claims.page: review of 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', Originality section

claims.claim: The same reviewer describes a layered unreliability in the Tawny Man narration in which every level of the narration is imperfect, including the narrating self.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel blog, review of The Golden Fool
claims.quote: every level of the narration is imperfect
claims.page: review of 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', final discussion paragraph
